newsitem.title: TURKEY: Political tensions batter wary Turkish shares.
newsitem.headline: Political tensions batter wary Turkish shares.

text.p: Turkish stocks dropped more than seven percent before recovering somewhat on Thursday over concerns the Islamist-led coalition was crumbling in the face of pressures from the secularist military, brokers said.

The IMKB National-100 closed at 1,457 -- down 4.9 percent -- recovering part of its losses in the afternoon in reaction buys. Turkish financial and capital markets reopened after a 6-1/2-day holiday for the Moslem Eid al-Adha festival and Children's Day.
"Purchases in reaction to the sharp morning fall emerged in the afternoon. But the market will remain negative as long as political uneasiness continues," said Goksin Teker from Taib Investment.
Political jitters ahead of a key meeting of the military-dominated National Security Council on April 26 and prospects for renewed political uncertainty also gripped money markets.

Bond rates rose by one to four points and the Turkish lira weakened to 134,050 against the dollar from the previous close of 132,600 on April 17. The central bank dollar sales helped the lira recover from a low of 134,270.
Press reports that the main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz had prepared alternative government models to replace the existing coalition dominated the market, brokers said.
Yilmaz, chairman of Motherland Party, offered two different government combinations, grouping several different parties.
Existing party leaders, seen by many as stumbling blocks to past deals, would be excluded from his formulas to take the country to elections in 1998 or 1999, daily Hurriyet reported.

Milliyet newspaper said MPs from both wings of the coalition considered withdrawal or resignation ahead of the meeting of the council, which earlier asked the government to implement regulations to combat rising Islamist activism.
However, Ahmet Tekdal, an assistant head of Erbakan's Welfare Party, said his party would stay in government despite mounting military-led pressure.
The military members of the council are expected to increase demands on the reluctant government to implement anti-Islamist measures introduced by the generals back in February.
"The index may drift sideways tomorrow but the market will set direction after the weekend's news," said Nazmi Sarikaya from Dis Securities.
Serdar Surer from Ekinciler Securities said political worries, accompanied by a liquidity shortage, would continue to set the tone for the market in the coming days.
Some brokers expect stock prices to rebound after the collapse of the government which they believe will pave the way for the establishment of a stronger coalition.
"The index may fall to the 1,350 level by the weekend. But I think the market will be relieved if the government collapses," Korhan Biricik from Deha Securities said.

Mustafa Arar, head of Ari Securities, said any new government to replace the troubled one would be considered as "a solution government" which will take necessary measures to overcome chronic economic and social problems before heading for new elections.
